preamble: A boy in the last year of primary school talks about the football game his class plays at break time. He is the one who goes in goal.
body:
I get there first, every break.
You have to, for the jumpers.
Two at their end, two at ours,
paced out with your feet so it's fair,
so nobody argues later when the ball
goes by the post and Kieran swears it was in.

I put myself in goal. Nobody put me there.
Dan does the picking because it's his ball,
and he said, anyone, and I said, me,
and he said, fine, go in.
So that's me choosing.

You can see everything from this end.
That's the bit people don't get.
Up there in the middle you spend the whole game
running at the back of somebody's head.
Back here I know who's tired,
who's got a stitch and won't say it,
who does the same trick every single time,
who looks at the ball too long before he goes.

Fourteen went past me last Tuesday.
I'm not ashamed of fourteen.
Four of them nobody alive could have saved.
One I let in on purpose, because Reece
has never scored in his life,
and you should have seen him after.
I could have had it. I had my hands
on it.

My mum asked if I ever get a go up front.
I told her I don't want one.
She said all right then, love.

Their end has proper netting,
knotted stuff the caretaker put up in March.
Ours is two jumpers and the air between them.
We still say net.
It hit the net. It's in the net.
Nobody has ever once said
there isn't one.

Dan picked me eighth last week. Out of eight.
He was being funny. I laughed as well.

Bell goes. I collect the jumpers,
mine, Reece's, Kieran's, the two blue ones,
and stack them by the fence for tomorrow.
I'm not shifting out of there.
Somebody has to keep the goal.
